```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# The calibration runs below take about 20 minutes on 8 cores, so the code
# chunks are not run when the vignette is built. Their results were saved by
# dev/precompute-calibration.R and are read from calibration-results.rds.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%")
library(crywolf)
results <- readRDS("calibration-results.rds")
```

A 95% credible interval should contain the true value in about 95% of
datasets. When the model is misspecified, it may not, and nothing in a
single fit will warn you. Simulation-based calibration answers the question
for a given design: simulate many datasets from known parameters, fit the
model to each, and count how often the intervals cover the truth.

## The workflow

1. Describe the design you can afford: number of sites, automated occasions,
   fraction of sites verified, and plausible detection and false-positive
   rates.
2. Describe the false-positive structure you suspect: homogeneous, random
   among sites, or tracking an environmental gradient.
3. Run `fp_calibrate()` with the candidate models.
4. Read the coverage and bias of the quantity you care about, usually the
   occupancy slope.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(crywolf)
fp_compile()   # compile once before starting parallel workers

future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 8)

design <- expand.grid(
  nsite = 300, nocc = 20, p10 = 0.05, frac_verified = 0.3,
  conf_effect = c(0, 0.5, 1.5), conf_cor = 0.7
)

cal <- fp_calibrate(
  design,
  models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_on_x = ~ x),
  occ = ~ x, reps = 50, parallel = TRUE
)
summary(cal)
```

The code above is not run when this vignette is built; the output below
comes from the same call, saved in advance. `summary()` prints, for the
occupancy slope, the coverage of the 95% intervals, its Monte Carlo standard
error, the bias, and a verdict:

```{r results-confusion, echo = FALSE}
summary(results$confusion)
```

```{r plot-confusion, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Coverage of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope against the strength of the confusion, for the constant-rate model and for a false-positive rate that depends on the occupancy covariate. Bars span two Monte Carlo standard errors; the dashed line is the nominal coverage."}
plot(results$confusion, by = "conf_effect")
```

Each replicate costs one Stan fit per model, so this design needs
3 cells × 50 replicates × 2 models = 300 fits. With 50 replicates, the Monte
Carlo standard error of a coverage of 0.95 is about 0.03, enough to tell a
calibrated model from a broken one; raise `reps` only to pin a borderline
value. Every model is fitted to the same datasets, so comparisons between
models are paired.

The column `prop_divergent` is the share of fits with at least one divergent
transition. In this run most fits had a few divergences (median 1 of 4000
draws), so check `max_rhat` and `divergences` in the returned tibble before
trusting a cell whose fits had many.

## How much to verify

Verification anchors the false-positive rate. It is natural to think that
verifying more sites will rescue a model that is not calibrated, and
`fp_verification_curve()` tests that directly:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fp_verification_curve(
  nsite = 300, nocc = 20, p10 = 0.05, conf_effect = 1.5, conf_cor = 0.7,
  frac_verified = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9),
  models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_on_x = ~ x),
  reps = 50, parallel = TRUE
)
```

```{r results-verification, echo = FALSE}
summary(results$verification)
```

```{r plot-verification, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Coverage of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope against the fraction of sites verified, under structured confusion (effect 1.5, correlation 0.7)."}
plot(results$verification)
```

## What to expect

In the simulation study that motivated this package (Provete et al., in
preparation), at a base false-positive rate of 0.05:

* When false positives were homogeneous, the constant-rate model kept nominal
  coverage of the occupancy slope. When they varied at random among sites,
  the estimate of the false-positive rate became unreliable, but coverage of
  the slope fell only to 0.81 (across all cells of that regime).
* When the false-positive rate tracked a gradient correlated with the
  occupancy covariate (effect 1.5 on the logit scale, correlation 0.7),
  coverage of the slope fell to 0.08–0.20, and verifying up to 90% of the
  sites did not restore it.
* Letting the false-positive rate depend on the occupancy covariate
  (`fp = ~ x`) recovered part of the coverage (0.48–0.66) and improved with
  verification; with the true gradient (`fp = ~ w`), coverage returned to
  0.90–0.97.
* Weak confusion (effects of 0.5 or less) left the constant-rate model
  calibrated at every correlation, including when false positives depended on
  the occupancy covariate itself.

So, if `fp_verification_curve()` shows the constant-rate model stuck below
nominal coverage, verifying more is not the remedy. Model the false-positive
rate instead, and verify enough to tell its effect apart from the occupancy
effect.

## Plotting

`plot()` draws the coverage of the occupancy slope against the design column
that varies (here, the fraction of sites verified), one colour per model,
with intervals of two Monte Carlo standard errors and a dashed line at the
nominal level. `type = "bias"` plots the bias instead, and `parameter`
selects another scored quantity. The result is a 'ggplot2' object that can be
modified as usual.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot(cal)
plot(cal, type = "bias")
plot(cal, parameter = "p10_bar")
```
